(Surah Saba' is Meccan, though it is said that the verse "And those who have been given knowledge see..." and what follows is an exception. It has fifty-four verses.)

﴿All praise is due to Allah, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ That is: to Him, Exalted is He, belongs, by creation, ownership and disposal through bringing into existence, annihilation, giving life and causing death, everything that exists in them, whether it is within their very reality or outside them while being established in them. It is as if it were said: all created things belong to Him, as was mentioned in the verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi). Describing Him, Exalted is He, with this is to confirm what the definite attributive of praise (al-hamd), with the definite article of genus (lam al-haqiqah), when linked to the Glorious Name, indicates: that all its instances are exclusively His, Exalted is He, as explained in the Opening of the Book, by making clear His unique oneness and His independent sufficiency in that which necessitates this. And every other existent, among which is man, lies under His dominion, Exalted is He; in its own essence it has no entitlement to existence, let alone to its other attributes. Rather, all of that is blessing overflowing upon it from Him, Mighty and Majestic. Whatever is of this condition is far removed from deserving praise, which is founded upon beauty proceeding from one who is capable and acts by choice. Thus the exclusivity of all its instances to Him, Exalted is He, becomes manifest. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the Hereafter﴾ is a statement of the exclusivity of praise in the Hereafter to Him, Exalted is He, following the statement of the exclusivity of praise in this world to Him. Moreover, the preposition phrase is related either to praise itself or to what the predicate depends upon, namely being established. Its being unrestricted from mention of that for which He is praised does not mean that mention of its being in the Hereafter suffices instead of specification, just as in what preceded, mention of the praised-for matter being in this world sufficed without mentioning that praise is also in this world. Rather, it is so that it encompasses the blessings of the Hereafter, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has fulfilled His promise to us and made us inherit the earth, that we may settle in the Garden wherever we will﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Who has settled us in the abode of permanence by His bounty﴾... the verse. And [praise for] worldly blessings that serve as a means to attaining them, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who has guided us to this﴾, that is: to that whose recompense is this—faith and righteous deeds. The difference between the two praises, given that the blessings of this world and the Hereafter are both by way of grace, is that the first is in the manner of worship, and the second in the manner of delight and gladness. It has been reported in a tradition that they are inspired to glorify [Allah] just as they are inspired to breathe.

﴿And He is the Wise﴾, who perfected the affairs of the religion and the world and arranged them as wisdom requires.

﴿the Acquainted﴾ with the inner aspects of things and their hidden realities. And His saying, Exalted is He:

(p-121) ﴿He knows what enters the earth﴾ ... and so on. This is a detailing of some of the matters encompassed by His knowledge, matters upon which their worldly and religious interests depend; that is, He knows what enters into it of rain, treasures, buried wealth, the dead, and the like.

﴿And what comes out of it﴾ such as animals, plants, the water of springs, and the like.

﴿And what descends from the sky﴾ such as the angels, the books, the decrees, and the like. It has been read as (wa-ma nunazzilu), with the doubling of the letter and the nun of majesty.

﴿And what ascends into it﴾ such as the angels, the deeds of the servants, the vapors, and the smokes.

﴿And He is the Most Merciful﴾ toward those who give thanks for the blessings He has mentioned, ﴿the Most Forgiving﴾ toward those who fall short in that, by His kindness and generosity.

The disbelievers say, ﴿The Hour will not come upon us.﴾ By the first-person pronoun they meant the whole of humankind, not only themselves or their contemporaries. By negating its coming they meant the complete negation of its existence, not merely its non-presence while it is actually realised. They expressed it this way because they had been promised its coming, and because the existence of future temporal events, especially the units of time, can only occur through coming and presence.

It is said that this is a mockery and sarcasm that expresses impatience for the promised coming, like their saying, "When is this promise?"

﴿Say, "Yes indeed."﴾ This is a rebuttal of their statement and an affirmation of what they denied, meaning that the matter is nothing but its coming. His saying, ﴿By my Lord, it will certainly come upon you,﴾ is an emphasis on this in the most complete and perfect manner.

It was read as (لِيَأْتِينَّكُمْ) (*liya'tiyannakum*, with the lam of command), based on interpreting the Hour as "the Day" or "the Time."

His saying, ﴿Knower of the unseen,﴾ and so on, is a reinforcement of the emphasis and a consolidation of it after a consolidation, and a breaking of the force of their denial and their disbelief. Following an oath with the most excellent attributes of the one sworn by, in absolute terms, indicates the magnificence of the matter sworn to and the strength of its establishment and soundness, because the one sworn by is in the position of a witness to the matter. There is no doubt that the more exalted and higher the witness, the more emphatic and stronger the testimony, and the more deserving of establishment and priority is the matter witnessed to. This is especially so when attributes that have a specific connection to the matter sworn to are singled out for mention, as in our case. Describing Him with knowledge of the unseen, whose most famous instances and most hidden elements are the matter sworn to, is an alert to them concerning the cause of the ruling and to the fact that it is something around which no trace of doubt whatsoever hovers. The benefit of commanding with this level of oath is that no excuse whatsoever remains for the obstinate ones, for they knew his trustworthiness and integrity, far removed from the stain of lying, let alone a false oath. They only failed to believe him out of arrogance.

It was read as (عَلّامُ الغَيْبِ) ('allāmu al-ghayb), (عالِمُ الغَيْبِ) ('ālimu al-ghayb), and (عالِمُ الغُيُوبِ) ('ālimu al-ghuyūb), in the nominative, as praise.

﴿Nothing escapes Him.﴾ That is, nothing is distant from Him. It was read with a kasra on the zay (لا يَعْزِبُ). ﴿The weight of an atom﴾ means the size of the smallest ant. ﴿In the heavens or in the earth﴾ means existing within them.

﴿Nor anything smaller than that﴾ means smaller than the weight of an atom, ﴿nor anything greater﴾ means greater than it. Both are in the nominative as inceptives (مُبْتَدَأ), and the predicate (خَبَر) is His saying, ﴿except that it is in a clear Record,﴾ which is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The sentence serves to emphasise the negation of escaping. It was read as (وَلا أصْغَرَ) and (وَلا أكْبَرَ) with a fatḥa on the rāʾ, to negate the category as a whole. It is not permissible to conjoin the nominative (مَرْفُوع) to (مِثْقالٍ), nor the accusative (مَفْتُوح) to (ذَرَّةٍ), because it is then in the position of the genitive, and it is barred from declension (al-sarf) because the exception (al-istithna') prevents it. The exception is only possible if the pronoun in (عَنْهُ) refers to the unseen (al-ghayb), and the recorded matter in the Tablet is considered outside of it, because it is manifest to those who read it. In that case the meaning is: nothing is separated from the unseen except that it is written down in the Tablet.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 4:

﴿That He may reward those who believed and did righteous deeds.﴾ This is a cause (ʿillah) for His saying, ﴿Surely it will come upon you﴾, and an explanation of what necessitates its coming.

﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring back to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul), in terms of their being characterized by what is in the sphere of the relative clause (silah). The distance implied in it (al-bu'd) serves to signal (li'l-idhan) the great distance of their rank in excellence and nobility. That is: those who are described by the sublime attributes.

﴿For them﴾, by virtue of that, ﴿is forgiveness﴾ for whatever shortcomings (furutat) of some kind they committed, which humans rarely are free from, ﴿and a noble provision﴾ in which there is no toil, and no reproach attached to it.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 5:**

﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾ by discrediting them and turning people away from believing in them.

﴿Striving to frustrate [Us]﴾: i.e., competing, so that they might escape Us. It is also recited as (*mu'jizin*), i.e., discouraging from faith whoever wishes to embrace it.

﴿For them is a punishment﴾: the discussion regarding it is like that which passed just above. The "min" in His words, exalted is He, ﴿of a painful kind (*rijz*)﴾ is explanatory (*lil-bayan*). Qatada, may Allah be pleased with him, said: *al-rijz* is the worst of punishment.

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿painful﴾ (*alim*), read in the nominative (*raf'*), it is an adjective of "punishment," i.e., those who strive for them have a punishment of the same kind as the worst punishment, severely painful. It is also recited in the genitive (*alimin*, *jarr*) as an adjective of *rijz*.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 6:

﴿And those who have been given knowledge see﴾ That is: the people of knowledge among the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and those among the scholars of the community who follow them, or those among the scholars of the People of the Book who believed, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, Kaʿb and their like, may God be pleased with them.

﴿that which has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ That is: the Qur'an.

﴿is the truth﴾ It is in the accusative (naṣb) as a second object of "yarā" (see), and the first object is the second relative pronoun, which is the pronoun of separation (ḍamīr al-faṣl). It has also been read in the nominative (rafʿ) as a subject (mubtadaʾ), with the predicate and the clause being the second object of "yarā." The Exalted statement "and yarā..." etc. is a resumed clause (mustaʾnaf), brought for the purpose of citing the people of knowledge against the ignorant who strive against the verses. It has also been said that it is in the accusative as a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "yajziya" (recompense), meaning: and that those of knowledge may know, at the coming of the Hour, by direct observation, that it is the truth, as they know it now through proof, and may argue with it against the deniers. It has also been permitted that by "people of knowledge" is meant those among the rabbis who did not believe, meaning: that they may know on that day that it is the truth, so they increase in regret and grief.

﴿and guides﴾ It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "al-ḥaqq" (the truth); the verb is conjoined to the noun because it is in its interpretation, as in the Exalted statement: ﴿those ranged in rows, and those who grasp﴾. That is: and grasping. As if it were said: "and those who have been given knowledge see that which has been sent down to you as the truth and as a guide."

﴿to the path of the Mighty, the Praiseworthy﴾ which is monotheism and clothing oneself in the garment of piety. It has also been said that it is a resumed clause; and it has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "that which has been sent down," with an implied subject, meaning: and He guides. As in the words of one who said:

"I escaped, and I left them as a pledge, Malik..."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 34, verse 7:**

﴿And those who disbelieve say﴾: they are the disbelievers of Quraysh, who said, addressing one another, ﴿Shall we direct you to a man﴾, meaning the Prophet (ﷺ). They intended by the indefinite form (*tankir*) mockery and derision. May God destroy them.

﴿Who will inform you﴾, that is, will tell you of a strange, wondrous thing. It is also read as (*yunbi'ukum*), from *al-inba'* (informing).

﴿When you are torn apart, every tearing﴾, that is, when you have died and your bodies are torn apart in every way and scattered in every manner, so that you become dust and crumbled bones.

﴿Indeed you are in a new creation﴾, that is, you will be settled in it. It was expressed as a nominal sentence (*al-jumla al-ismiyya*) instead of a verbal sentence that indicates occurrence, such as *tub'athun* (you will be raised) or *tukhlaqun khalqan jadidan* (you will be created a new creation), for the sake of emphasis in expressing disbelief and astonishment. Likewise, the adverbial phrase (*al-zarf*) is placed first, and its governing element (*al-'amil fihi*) is what is indicated by the mentioned term, not the term itself, because what follows *inna* does not govern what precedes it. *Jadid* is on the pattern *fa'il* in the sense of *fa'il* (active): from *jadda*, so it is *jadid*, as *qalla* gives *qalil*. It has also been said that it is in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive), from *jadda al-nassaj al-thawb* (the weaver cut the cloth) when he cut it, and then the usage spread.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 8:

﴿Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?﴾ That is, in what he said.

﴿Or is there madness in him?﴾ That is, insanity which makes them imagine this and which casts it upon his tongue. The use of this disjunction as evidence that there is an intermediate between truth and falsehood, namely what does not come from informing based on insight, is correct, since it is evident that fabrication (iftira') is more specific than lying (kadhib).

﴿But those who do not believe in the Hereafter are in punishment and far-off error.﴾ This is a response from Allah the Exalted to their disjunctive question, which was posed in the form of a question, by rejecting both of its parts (idrab 'an shiqqayhi) and nullifying them, and by affirming a third category that reveals the reality of the situation, censures their evil state, and points to their affliction with what they said about him (ﷺ). It is as if it were said: the matter is not as they claim; rather, they are in complete derangement of intellect and utmost straying from understanding, and in the perception which is madness in reality, and in the punishment that results from that. For this reason they say what they say. The mention of the punishment before what necessitates and entails it (i.e., the error) is for the sake of hastening to clarify what distresses them, and weakening their resolve, and indicating the extreme speed with which it follows from it, as if it were racing it and outpacing it. Describing the error with "far" (al-bu'd), which is a description of the one who errs, is for emphasis (mubalaghah). Placing the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the position of their pronoun is to draw attention, through what is in the relative clause, to the fact that the cause of what they committed and dared to do of the dreadful abomination is their disbelief in the Hereafter and the various kinds of punishment in it; and were it not for this, they would not have done that out of fear of its harm. His, the Exalted's, statement:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 9:

﴿Have they not looked at what is before them and what is behind them of the heaven and the earth?﴾ This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) aimed at magnifying the enormity of their audacity in denying the signs of God Most High, and at magnifying what they said concerning Him (ﷺ), and that this is among the grave matters that necessitate the descent of the most severe punishment and the arrival of the most dreadful torment without delay or postponement. The "fa" (fa') is for conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied antecedent that the context requires, and the saying of God Most High: ﴿If We will﴾ ... etc. is an explanation of what the mention of their being encompassed by them (the heaven and the earth) indicates of the feared harm expected from both of them. In it is an alert that nothing remains of the causes of its occurrence except the attachment of the divine will to it. That is: Have they done what they have done of the great reprehensible deed that entails punishment, and so have not looked at what encompasses them from all their sides, such that there is no escape for them from it and no refuge? ﴿If We will﴾, in accordance with what their crimes require.

﴿We would cause the earth to swallow them up﴾, as We caused it to swallow Qarun.

﴿Or We would make pieces of the sky fall upon them﴾, that is: pieces.

﴿from the sky﴾, as We made it fall upon the People of the Thicket (al-Aykah), because they deserved that for the crimes they committed. It is said: it is a reminder of what they witness of signs that indicate the perfection of His power, and what may contain a removal of their doubt about resurrection, to the point that they made it fabrication and mockery, and a threat upon it. The meaning: Have they been blind and not looked at what encompasses them from all sides, from the sky and the earth, and have they not reflected whether they are stronger in creation, or it (the sky)? And ﴿If We will, We would cause the earth to swallow them up or make pieces of the sky fall upon them﴾ is due to their denial of the signs after the clear proofs had appeared, so reflect. And be the manifest truth. It was read: (yakhsif) (p-124) and (yusqit) with the ya', in accordance with His saying: ﴿Has he invented against God?﴾ And (kisfan) with the sin sukun.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, that is: in what has been mentioned of the heaven and the earth, from the standpoint of their encompassing the observer from all sides, or in what has been recited of the revelation speaking of what has been mentioned.

﴿is surely a sign﴾, clear, ﴿for every servant who turns back (muneeb)﴾, whose disposition is to turn back to his Lord. For when he reflects upon them, or upon the aforementioned revelation, he restrains himself from indulging in vices and turns to Him, the Most High. In it is a powerful exhortation to repentance and turning back, and this has been emphasized by His saying, Most High:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 10:

﴿And We had certainly given David favour from Us.﴾ That is: We gave him this on account of his good return (to Us) and the soundness of his repentance, a favour (fadlan) over all the other prophets, peace be upon them, that is, a kind of favour. This is what is mentioned afterwards, for it is a miracle specific to him (ﷺ). Or (it means) over all people, and so it includes prophethood, the Scripture, kingship and a beautiful voice. Hence its indefiniteness (in the Arabic, fadlan, "a favour") is for magnification. And "from Us" (minna) serves to emphasise his intrinsic grandeur by his grandeur in being attributed to Us, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and We taught him knowledge from Us﴾. And placing it (fadlan) before the direct object is for the sake of giving importance to what is placed first and creating anticipation for what is delayed. For that which by rights should be placed first, when it is delayed, leaves the soul expectant of it, and when it arrives there, it settles in with greater firmness. ﴿O mountains, echo back with him﴾ from ta'wib (returning), that is: repeat with him the glorification, or the lamentation over the sin. This may be either by God Almighty creating in them a sound like his voice, just as He created speech in the tree, or by that appearing to him as such. It has also been read (ʾawwibī) from al-awb (returning), that is: return with him in glorification whenever he returns to it. And whenever he glorified, peace be upon him, he would hear from the mountains what is heard from one who glorifies, as a miracle for him, peace be upon him. It was said: he used to lament over his sin with a melodious and mournful cadence, and the mountains would assist him in his lamentation with their echoes, and the birds with their voices. It is a substitute (badal) for "We gave" by an implied "We said", or a substitute for "favour" by an implied "our saying". ﴿And the birds﴾ in the accusative, conjoined to "favour", meaning: and We subjected the birds to him; because their being given to him, peace be upon him, is their being subjected to him, so there is no need to imply it, as is reported from al-Kisa'i. Nor is there need to posit an elided noun, that is, "the glorification of the birds", as is reported from him in one narration. It was said: conjoined to the place (mahall) of "the mountains", and in this there is an artificiality in wording and meaning that is not hidden. It is also read in the nominative, conjoined to its wording, likening the incidental built-in vowel to the grammatical (i'rabi) vowel. The accusative has also been permitted as an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ahu), but the first is the preferred view. In presenting the mountains and birds as rational beings obedient to His command and submissive to His judgment, there is an indication that there is no animal, inanimate thing, mute or speaking, except that it is submitted to His will and not resistant to His desire, a magnificence expressing the utmost greatness of His majesty and the perfection of His sovereign grandeur, which is not hidden from people of understanding.

﴿And We made iron soft for him﴾ That is: We made it pliable in itself like wax, which he shapes in his hand however he wishes, without heating it with fire or striking it with a hammer. Or: We made it soft relative to his strength, which We had given him, as wax is soft relative to the other human powers.

﴿That work﴾: We commanded him, "Work," where "an" is a verbal (masdariyya, "infinitival") particle from which the preposition *bāʾ* has been dropped. Taking it as an explanatory (mufassira) "an" involves a strain that is not hidden.

﴿Full-length﴾: wide. It was also read as (ṣābighāt), and these are wide, flowing coats of mail. He, peace be upon him, was the first to make them, and before that they were plates. They said: When he became king over the Children of Israel, he used to go out in disguise and ask people, "What do you say about Dawud?" and they would praise him. Then God Most High appointed for him an angel in the form of a human being, who asked him as was his custom. He said, "What an excellent man, were it not for one trait in him." Dawud was alarmed and asked him about it. He said, "Were it not that he feeds his dependents from the public treasury." At that, he asked his Lord to provide him with the means to be independent of the public treasury. So God Most High taught him the craft of making coats of mail. It was also said: He used to sell coats of mail for four thousand (dirhams), spending from them on himself and his dependents, and giving charity to the poor.

﴿And measure well in the weaving﴾: *al-sard* is the weaving of coats of mail, i.e., be moderate in weaving them so that their rings are proportionate. It was also said: "Measure well in its rivets," so do not make them thin or thick. This was refuted on the grounds that his coats of mail, peace be upon him, were not riveted, as the softening of the iron indicates. It was also said: The meaning of "measure well in the weaving" is: do not devote all your time to it, but only as much as is needed to obtain your sustenance, and devote the rest to worship. This is most appropriate to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And work righteousness﴾, where the address is general, in accordance with the generality of the obligation upon him, peace be upon him, and upon his family.

﴿Indeed I am Seeing of what you do﴾: This is a reason for the command, or for the obligation of complying with it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 12:

﴿And to Solomon the wind⦆ — that is: We subjected the wind to him. It is also read with the wind in the nominative (raf‘, i.e., grammatically rendered as "al-rīḥu"), meaning "And for Solomon the wind is subjected," and it is read: (al-riyāḥa) (the winds, in the accusative plural).

﴿Its morning course is a month's journey and its evening course is a month's journey﴾ — that is: its course in the morning covers the distance of a month's journey, and its course in the evening likewise. The clause is either a new independent sentence, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the wind. It is also read: (ghadwatuhā) and (rawḥatuhā). It is related from al-Ḥasan, may Allah have mercy on him, that he would set out in the morning from Damascus, take his midday rest at Istakhr, then go on in the afternoon, so that his afternoon was at Kabul. It is also said: he would take his midday meal at al-Rayy and his evening meal at Samarqand. It is related that some people saw an inscription in a dwelling in the region of the Tigris, written by one of the companions of Solomon, peace be upon him: "We alighted in it, and we did not build it; and we found it built. We set out from Istakhr in the morning, and we spoke of it; and we are returning from it in the afternoon, and we will spend the night in Syria, if Allah the Exalted wills."

﴿And We caused a fount of copper to flow for him﴾ — that is: molten copper, which He caused to flow from its ore, just as He softened iron for David, peace be upon them both. So it gushed forth like water gushing from a spring, and for this reason it was called a "fount" (‘ayn). This was in Yemen. It is also said that it flowed for three days each month. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And among the jinn were those who worked before him⦆ is either a complete nominal sentence (mubtada’ and khabar), or "those who worked" is conjoined to "the wind," and "among the jinn" is a preposed circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

﴿By the permission of his Lord﴾ — by His command, exalted is He, as His statement indicates: ﴿And whoever of them deviates from Our command﴾ — that is: whoever of them departs from what We commanded him regarding obedience to Solomon. It is also read: (yuzigh), in the passive form, from (azāghahu) (to cause him to deviate).

﴿We shall make him taste the punishment of the Blaze﴾ — that is: the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter. It is related from al-Suddi, may Allah have mercy on him, that there was an angel with him holding a whip of fire; whoever disobeyed him, he would strike, from a place the jinn could not see.

﴿They made for him whatever he willed﴾ is an elaboration of what was mentioned of their work. His words, exalted is He, ﴿of sanctuaries﴾ ... etc., explain "whatever he willed," meaning: of strong fortresses and noble dwellings. They were so named because they are defended and fought over. It has also been said that they are the mosques.

﴿and statues﴾: images of the angels and prophets, peace be upon them, in the form they were accustomed to, for these were made in the mosques at that time so that people would see them and worship in the manner of their worship. The prohibition of images is a new law (shar' jadid). It is narrated that they made two lions at the base of his throne and two eagles above it. When he wanted to ascend, the two lions would stretch out their forelegs, and when he sat, the two eagles would shade him with their wings.

﴿and bowls﴾, the plural of *jafna*, which is a large dish.

﴿like watering-troughs﴾: like large cisterns, the plural of *jabiya* (basin), from *al-jibaya* (gathering), because water gathers in them. It is one of the predominantly adjectival nouns, like *al-dabba* (beast). It was also read with the *ya'* affirmed. It has been said that a thousand men could sit upon one bowl.

﴿and cauldrons fixed firmly﴾: fixed in place on their hearth-stones, not moved from them because of their great size.

﴿Work, family of David, in thankfulness﴾ is a report of what was said to them. "Thankfulness" (*shukran*) is in the accusative, and it may be a direct object (*maf'ul lahu*, object of purpose), or an infinitive (*masdar*) of "work," because working for the benefactor is thanks to him, or of an implied verb, meaning: give thanks with thanks. Or it is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), meaning: giving thanks. Or it is a direct object: work thankfulness.

﴿And few of My servants are truly grateful﴾: that is, one who devotes himself to rendering thanks with his heart, tongue and limbs for most of his time, and even with that he does not fulfill its due, because being granted the ability to give thanks is a blessing that calls for another thanks, without end. For this reason it has been said: the most grateful (*al-shakur*) is one who sees his inability to give thanks. It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, divided the hours of the night and day among his family, so that no hour of the hours would come except that a person from the family of David was standing and praying.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 14:

﴿When We decreed death upon him﴾, that is, upon Sulayman, peace be upon him.

﴿Nothing showed them﴾, that is, the jinn or their agents, ﴿his death except a creature of the earth﴾, that is, the termite (al-arada), which is attributed to its action. It is also read with a fatha on the ra' (al-araḍa), and it means the wood's being affected by its action. It is said: the termite ate (araḍat) the wood, a gnawing (ard), so the wood was eaten (fa-ṣirat aradan), like the molars ate his teeth, a chewing (akl), so they were chewed (fa-ukilat akla).

﴿eating away at his staff﴾, that is, his staff, from nasa'tu al-ba'ir, when you drove the camel away, because it is used to drive away whatever is driven away. It is also read as (minsātahu) with a static alif in place of the hamza, with a static hamza, and with the hamza pronounced between its two sounds (bayna bayna) when stopping (al-waqf). And (minsā'atahu) follows the pattern mif'ālah, like mīḍā'ah for mīḍa'ah, and min sātihi, that is, from the tip of his staff, from sa'at al-qaws (the bow's tip); in it there are two dialects, as in qiḥah with kasra and with fatha. It is also read: (akalat minsātahu).

﴿So when he fell, the jinn became clear﴾, from tabayyantu al-shay' when you knew it after it had been obscure to you, that is, the jinn came to know clearly after the matter had been obscure to them.

﴿that had they known the unseen, they would not have remained in the humiliating punishment﴾, that is, that if they had known the unseen as they claim, they would have known of his death, peace be upon him, at the moment it occurred, and so they would not have remained after him for a year in subjugating him until he fell. Or it is from tabayyana al-shay' when it became manifest and clear, that is, the jinn became manifest. And anna (that) together with what is within its scope is a badl ishtimal (inclusive apposition, a substitute that encompasses its antecedent) for al-jinn, that is, it became manifest that the jinn, ﴿if they had known the unseen﴾… etc. It is also read: (tubayyinat al-jinn) in the passive form, on the basis that the one made clear in reality is anna together with what is within its scope, because it is a substitute. It is also read: (tabayyanat al-ins), and the pronoun in kanū refers to the jinn in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and among the jinn are those who work﴾. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: (the humans came to know that the jinn, had they known the unseen…).

It is narrated that Dawud, peace be upon him, laid the foundations of the building of Bayt al-Maqdis at the site of the tent of Musa, but he died before its completion. He bequeathed it to Sulayman, peace be upon them both, and he employed the jinn and the devils in it, and they laboured on it until his appointed time drew near and he knew of it. He asked his Lord to conceal his death from them until they finished it, and so that their claim of knowing the unseen would be refuted. He summoned them, and they built over him a palace of glass with no door. He stood praying, leaning on his staff, and his soul was taken while he was leaning upon it, so he remained thus, and they were occupied with what they had been commanded of the works, until the termite ate his staff and he fell dead. The devils used to gather around his prayer niche (miḥrab) wherever he was, and no devil would look at him during his prayer without being burned. One day a devil passed by him and looked, and behold, Sulayman, peace be upon him, had fallen dead. They opened it up for him, and behold, his staff had been eaten by the termite. They wanted to know the time of his death, so they placed the termite on the staff, and it ate from it a certain amount in a day and a night. They calculated on that basis and found that he had died a year earlier. His age was fifty-three years. He became king at the age of thirteen, and he remained in his kingdom for forty years, and he began building Bayt al-Maqdis four years into his reign.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 15:

﴿There was indeed for Saba' (Sheba)﴾ is an explanation, serving to relate what some of the disbelievers did with the blessings of God, immediately after the description of the states of those who give thanks for them. That is, for the descendants of Saba' ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. It has been read with the diptote form (mamnu' min al-sarf), as the name of a tribe. It has also been read with the hamza converted into an alif, and perhaps this is a rendering of it as an intermediate sound (bayn bayn). ﴿in their dwelling-place﴾. It has also been read with a kasra on the kaf, like al-masjid, and it has been read in the plural form, meaning the places of their residence. It was in Yemen. It is called Ma'rib, and between it and San'a' is a distance of three nights' journey.

﴿a sign﴾, indicating, by considering its past and future circumstances, the existence of the Maker, the Chooser, the One Able to do whatever He wills of wondrous matters, who rewards the good-doer and the evildoer, supporting the proof mentioned earlier, as in the stories of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them both.

﴿two gardens﴾ is either an apposition (badal) to "sign," or a predicate of an omitted subject, that is, "it is two gardens." There is in it the sense of praise, and the reading in the accusative as an expression of praise supports this. What is meant by the two are two groups of gardens.

﴿on the right and on the left﴾: a group to the right of their town, and a group to its left, each of these two groups being close to the other and joined together, as if they were one garden. Or, the two gardens are each man's garden, on the right of his dwelling and on its left.

﴿Eat of the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him﴾ is a report of what was said to them through the tongue of their Prophet, to complete the blessing and to remind them of its rights. Or it is what the tongue of their state spoke. Or it is an explanation that they were worthy of being told this.

﴿A good land and a Lord who is Forgiving﴾ is a resumed statement clarifying what necessitates the thanks commanded, that is: your town is a good town, and your Lord, who provided you with the good things in it and who required thanks from you, is a Forgiving Lord toward the shortcomings of those who give Him thanks. All of it has been read in the accusative as an expression of praise. It is said: it was the best of lands in air and in fertility, and a woman would go out with a basket on her head, working with her hands and walking among the trees, and the basket would fill with the fruits that fell into it, and there was no harmful vermin in it at all.

﴿فَأعْرَضُوا﴾ [So they turned away] from gratitude after the signs that called them to it had been made clear. It is said: Allah sent to them thirteen prophets, who called them to Allah, reminded them of His blessings, and warned them of His punishment, but they denied them.

﴿فَأرْسَلْنا عَلَيْهِمْ سَيْلَ العَرِمِ﴾ [So We sent against them the flood of al-'Arim]. That is, the flood of the severe matter, meaning the harsh one, from "'arama al-rajul," so he is 'arim, when his disposition becomes ill-tempered and difficult; or it means the violent rain. It is said: al-'Arim is the plural of 'urmah, which is piled-up stones. It is said: it is the dam that holds back the water. It is said: it is the name of the structure that is made into a barrier. It is said: it is the sturdy structure that the queen Bilqis built between the two mountains with rock and pitch, and in which she collected the water of springs and rains, and in which she left openings for what they needed for their irrigation (p-128). It is said: al-'Arim is the rat that gnawed through that dam for them, the blind mouse called the mole. Allah the Exalted empowered it against their dam, so it gnawed through it and drowned their lands. It is said: al-'Arim is the name of the valley. It was also read as (al-'ARM) with a sukun on the ra'. They said: this happened in the interval (fatrah) between 'Isa and the Prophet, upon both of them be prayer and peace.

﴿وَبَدَّلْناهم بِجَنَّتَيْهِمْ﴾ [And We exchanged for them their two gardens]. That is, We removed their two gardens and gave them in their place (two others).

﴿جَنَّتَيْنِ ذَواتَيْ أُكُلٍ خَمْطٍ﴾ [two gardens bearing bitter produce]. That is, fruit that is unpalatable, for khamt is every plant that has taken on a taste of bitterness so that it cannot be eaten. It is said: it is the sour and bitter of everything. It is said: it is the fruit of a tree called faswat al-dab', in the form of poppy seed, from which no benefit is obtained. It is said: it is the arak tree and every thorny tree. The implied sense is: "ukulin ukuli khamt," so the modified noun was deleted and the modifier was put in its place. It was also read as (ukuli khamt) with the idafah and with ukul lightened.

﴿وَأثْلٍ وشَيْءٍ مِن سِدْرٍ قَلِيلٍ﴾ [and tamarisk, and a little lote-tree]. These two are conjoined to ukul, not to khamt, for al-athl is the tamarisk. It is said: it is a tree resembling it but larger, and it has no fruit. It was also read as (wa athlan) and (shay'an), conjoined to "two gardens." It is said: He described the lote-tree as few because what is picked from it, which is the nabq, is edible and sweet, and for this reason it is planted in orchards. The correct view is that the lote-tree is of two kinds: one kind whose fruit is eaten and whose leaves are used for washing the hands, and another kind whose fruit is astringent and not eaten at all, and whose leaves are not used, which is the wild lote (al-dal). The intended one here is certainly the second. Qatadah said: their trees were the best of trees, but Allah turned them into the worst of trees because of their deeds. Naming the replacements "two gardens" is by way of *mushakalah* (matching of expression, a rhetorical correspondence of wording) and mockery (tahakkum).

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ ("That") is a demonstrative referring either to the verbal noun (masdar) of the phrase ﴿جَزَيْنَاهُمْ﴾ ("We requited them"), or to the mentioned exchange (al-tabdil) together with the sense of distance in it, to signal how far its degree of atrocity extends. Its grammatical position, according to the first view, is in the accusative (nasb) as a verbal noun (masdar) serving as an emphatic (mu'akkid) for the verb mentioned. According to the second view, it is in the accusative as a second object (maf'ul thani) of the verb. The meaning is: "That atrocious recompense is what We requited them with, not any other recompense," or "That exchange is what We requited them with, not anything else."

﴿بِمَا كَفَرُوا﴾ ("for their ingratitude") means: because of their ingratitude for the blessing, in that We took it away from them and put its opposite in its place. Or it means: because of their disbelief in the messengers.

﴿وَهَلْ نُجَازِي إِلَّا الْكَفُورَ﴾ ("And do We requite any but the ungrateful?") means: We do not requite with this recompense anyone except the one who is extreme in ingratitude or disbelief. It is also recited as ﴿يُجَازِي﴾ with the verb in the active voice, its subject being Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It is also recited as ﴿يُجَازَى﴾ in the passive voice, with ﴿الْكَفُورُ﴾ in the nominative, and as ﴿يُجْزَى﴾ in the passive voice as well. This passage explains the blessings they were given that were present in their dwellings, what they did with them of ingratitude, and the recompense that was inflicted on them. Then His statement, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 18:

﴿And We placed between them and the towns which We had blessed⁠﴾ is a narration of the blessings that they were given, which were manifest in their journeys and their trading, and of the ingratitude (kufran) they committed with them and what befell them because of that; it completes their story and explains their outcome. The whole was not mentioned together because of the (benefit of) dualism (al-tathniyah), and repetition brings added alertness and reminder. It is conjoined (ʿatf) to "There was a sign for Saba'" (kana li-Saba'), not to what follows it of sentences that speak of their deeds or their recompense. That is: And We placed, along with what We had given them in their dwellings of various kinds of blessings, between them, that is between their lands, and between the Syrian towns which We had blessed for the worlds.

﴿Towns, visible⁠﴾ connected, some of them visible from others because of their proximity, so they are visible to the eyes of their inhabitants; or riding the road's back, visible to travelers, not far from their routes, so that they would not be hidden from them.

﴿And We determined therein the travel⁠﴾ that is, We made them, in the ratio of some to others, at a specific measure suited to the condition of the wayfarers. It was said: whoever set out in the morning from one town would take a midday rest in another, and whoever set out in the evening would spend the night in another, until he reached Syria. All of that was a completion of the kinds of favor they had been given, and an abundance of them in both settled life and travel.

﴿Travel therein⁠﴾ on the understanding of a saying: that is, and We said to them, "Travel in those towns."

﴿Nights and days⁠﴾ that is, whenever you wish, of the nights and days.

﴿Secure⁠﴾ from everything you dislike; the security therein does not vary with the variation of times. Or: travel therein secure, even if the duration of your journey lengthens and its nights and days become many; or: travel therein for the nights and days of your lives, meeting nothing there but security, yet not in actual reality but by way of treating their enablement to the mentioned travel, and the equalizing of its beginnings and causes in the mentioned manner, as equivalent to commanding them to that.

﴿So they said, "Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys farther apart."﴾ It is also read: (O our Lord). They became ungrateful for the blessing, grew weary of the finest living, and disliked ease, so they sought hardship and toil, just as the Children of Israel asked for garlic and onions in place of the manna and quails. They said: "If the fruits of our gardens were farther away, we would be more inclined to desire them." They asked Allah, exalted is He, to place between them and al-Sham (Greater Syria) deserts and wastelands, so that they could ride their mounts through them, take provisions, and show off over the poor. So Allah, exalted is He, hastened to answer them by ruining those intermediate settlements and making them a barren waste in which no caller is heard and no one answers. It is also read: "Ba'ada" and "Rabbana: ba'id bayna asfarina" and "wa ba'ada baynu asfarina," with the verb addressed as a vocative, and with the verb attributed to bayna (between) and bayna being its grammatical subject, as one says: "sira farsakhan" (two farsakhs were traveled) and "bu'ida bayna asfarina" (the distance between our journeys was made far). It is also read: "Rabbana (ba'id bayna asfarina)" and "(bayna safarina)." And "ba'ada" with "Rabbuna" in the nominative, as the subject (mubtada'), and the meaning is the opposite of the first reading, namely that they considered it far-fetched to travel through these places even though they were short or near, and easy to traverse, because of their extreme luxury, their utmost affluence, and their failure to acknowledge the blessings of Allah, exalted is He, as though they were disputing with Allah, exalted is He, and grieving against Him.

﴿And they wronged themselves﴾ by exposing themselves to wrath and punishment when they became ungrateful for the blessing or disregarded it.

﴿So We made them tales﴾ meaning: We made them such that people speak of them, marveling at their conditions and taking warning from their end and fate.

﴿And We tore them completely apart﴾ meaning: We scattered them in every kind of dispersal, with "mumazzaq" being a verbal noun, or "every place and location of dispersal," with it being a noun of place. In the expression "tamzeeq," which specifically refers to tearing apart what is connected and separating it, there is an exaggeration of the matter and an indication of the severity of the impact and the pain, which is clear. That is, We tore them apart with a tearing beyond which there is no further limit, such that they became proverbial in every separate group, with no reunion after them, until Ghassan joined al-Sham, Anmar joined Yathrib, Judham joined Tihamah, and the Azd joined Oman. The origin of their story, as narrated by al-Kalbi from Abu Salih, is that Amr ibn Amir was one of the descendants of Saba', and between them were twelve fathers. He is the one who is called Muzaiqiya ibn Ma' al-Sama'. Tarifa the soothsayer informed him of the ruin of the Dam of Ma'rib and the scattering of the flood of al-Arim, which destroyed the two gardens. According to Abu Zayd al-Ansari, Amr saw a gnawing rodent gnawing at the dam, so he knew that it would not endure after that. It was said that he was a soothsayer and knew this through his soothsaying, so he sold his properties and set out with his people, who were thousands, from one land to another until he reached the honored city of Makkah and its people, Jurhum, who had subdued the people and seized authority over the House from the sons of Isma'il (peace be upon him) and others. So he sent to them Tha'laba ibn Amr ibn Amir, asking them to let him stay with them until his scouts, whom he had sent to the far regions of the lands to seek a place for him and his people that would accommodate them, returned to him, but they refused. They fought for three days, and Jurhum was defeated, and none of them escaped except the fugitive. Tha'laba stayed in Makkah and its surroundings with his people and armies for a year. Then fever struck them, and they were compelled to leave, and his scouts had returned to him, so they split into two groups. One group headed toward Oman, and they were the Azd, Kindah, Himyar, and those who followed them. Tha'laba headed toward al-Sham, and the Aws and Khazraj, the two sons of Haritha ibn Tha'laba, settled in Madinah, and they are the Ansar. Ghassan went on and settled in al-Sham. Khuza'a withdrew and settled in Makkah, where Rabi'a ibn Haritha ibn Amr ibn Amir, who was Luhayy, remained. He took charge of Makkah and the custodianship of the House. Then the descendants of Isma'il (peace be upon him) came to them and asked them to let them live with them and around them, and they permitted them to do so. It was narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that Farwa ibn Musayk al-Ghutayfi asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about Saba'. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "He was a man who had ten sons. Six of them settled in Yemen: Madhhij, Kindah, the Azd, the Ash'aris, Himyar, and Anmar, from whom are Bujayla and Khath'am. Four of them settled in al-Sham: Lakhm, Judham, Amilah, and Ghassan. When their wealth perished and their lands were ruined, they were scattered in every direction. Some groups of them settled in the Hijaz. Among them was Khuza'a, who settled on the outskirts of Makkah, and the Aws and Khazraj settled in Yathrib. They were the first to inhabit it. Then three tribes of Jews settled with them: Banu Qaynuqa', Banu Qurayza, and al-Nadir. They formed alliances with the Aws and Khazraj and stayed with them. Other groups settled in al-Sham, and they are those who later became Christians: Ghassan, Amilah, Lakhm, Judham, Tanukh, Taghlib, and others. Saba' encompasses all these tribes." The majority view is that all the Arabs are of two divisions: Qahtaniyya and Adnaniyya. The Qahtaniyya have two branches: Saba' and Hadramawt. The Adnaniyya have two branches: Rabi'a and Mudar. As for Qudā'a, there is disagreement about it: some attribute them to Qahtan, and some to Adnan. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best.

﴿Indeed in that﴾ meaning: in what has been mentioned of their story ﴿are signs﴾ great ones ﴿for everyone who is steadfast and grateful﴾, meaning: his nature is patience in restraining desires and the impulses of whim, and in bearing the hardships of acts of obedience, and gratitude for blessings. The specification of these people with this is because they are the ones who benefit from them.

﴿And Iblis indeed found his assumption about them to be true﴾. That is, he made his assumption about them come true, or found it to be correct. It was also recited with the lightened form (takhfif, reciting the doubled letter as a single one), meaning: he was right in his assumption, or he was right through an assumption he had made. It is permissible for the verb to take its object directly, because the assumption is a kind of speech. It was also recited with ﴿Iblis﴾ in the accusative and ﴿his assumption﴾ in the nominative with tashdid (doubling), meaning: his assumption found him to be truthful. With takhfif it means: he told him the truth when he imagined to him their being led astray. It was also recited with both words in the nominative. The takhfif is by way of substitution (ibdal, replacing one element with another). This is either his assumption about Saba' when he saw their immersion in desires, or his assumption about the children of Adam when he saw Adam, peace be upon him, had given ear to his whispering. He said: their offspring are weaker in resolve than he was. It was also said: he made this assumption when God Most High informed the angels that He would place in the earth one who would cause corruption in it and shed blood. And he said: ﴿I will surely mislead them, and I will surely lead them astray﴾.

﴿So they followed him﴾. That is, the people of Saba' or mankind.

﴿except a group of the believers﴾. That is, except a group who are the believers and did not follow him, with "min" (من) being explanatory (bayaniyya, i.e., "min" in the sense of "namely"). Their smallness is in comparison with the disbelievers. Or it means: except a group from among the groups of the believers who did not follow him, and they are the sincere ones (al-mukhlisun).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 21:

﴿And he had no authority over them﴾, i.e., no domination (taslluṭ) and seizing (istīlā') by whispering (waswasa) and enticement (al-istiwā').(p-131) And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except that We might make evident who believes in the Hereafter from who is in doubt concerning it﴾ is an exceptive construction (istithnā' mufarragh) from the causal particle (min a'lam al-'ilal), and "man" (who) is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla), meaning: his domination over them was only so that Our knowledge would relate to the one who believes in the Hereafter, distinguished from the one who is in doubt concerning it, a present relation (ta'alluq ḥālī) upon which the recompense is based; or "except that the believer might be distinguished from the doubter"; or "except that he who has been decreed to believe might believe, and he who has been decreed to be astray might doubt." The intended meaning of the attainment of knowledge is the attainment of its object, as an intensification (mubālagha).

﴿And your Lord is Guardian over all things﴾, i.e., Preserver of them (muḥāfiẓ 'alayhi). For fa'īl and mufā'il are two mutually akin forms (ṣīghatān mutā'akhiyatān).

﴿Say﴾: that is, to the polytheists, to make manifest the falsehood of what they hold, and to rebuke them.

﴿Call upon those whom you claimed﴾: that is, whom you claimed to be gods. These are the two objects of "zaʿama" (claimed). The first was elided for lightness, due to the length of the relative clause with its complement, and the second because its qualifier stands in its place, namely His saying, exalted is He, ﴿besides Allah﴾. It is not possible to make it the second object, because it does not form a coherent sentence with the pronoun. Likewise "they do not possess" is not parsed as such, because they do not claim it for them. The meaning is: call upon them in matters that concern you, whether bringing about benefit or warding off harm, so that perhaps they will respond to you, if your claim is correct. Then He answered on their behalf, indicating that the answer is determined and that it does not admit of obstinacy, saying: ﴿They do not possess the weight of an atom﴾ of good or evil, benefit or harm ﴿in the heavens or in the earth﴾: that is, in any matter whatsoever. He mentioned both for generality by convention, or because some of their gods are heavenly, such as the angels and the stars, and some earthly, such as the idols, or because the proximate causes of good and evil are heavenly and earthly. The clause is a resumptive statement explaining their condition. ﴿And they have not﴾: that is, their gods.

﴿In them is no partnership﴾: that is, a partnership neither of creation, nor of ownership, nor of management.

﴿And there is not for Him﴾: that is, for Allah, exalted is He.

﴿from among them﴾: from among their gods ﴿any supporter﴾ who assists Him in managing their affair.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 23:

﴿And intercession with Him will not benefit [anyone]﴾. That is: it does not exist at all, as in his saying: "And you do not see the lizard (dabb) go into its burrow [when it is seized]" [meaning: it does not go in at all].

Because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ The negation was attached to its benefit rather than to its occurrence, explicitly negating what they intended from its occurrence. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except for one whom He permits﴾ is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from the most general of states (a'amm al-ahwal). That is: intercession occurs in no state except being for the one to whom He has given permission to intercede, from among the prophets, the angels and their like, from among those worthy of the station of intercession. Thus the disbelievers' deprivation of it is made clear, completely. As for their idols, it is evident that permission for them is absent, since permission for intercession is impossible for an inanimate object that neither understands nor speaks. As for those whom they worship among the angels, their permission is restricted to intercession for those who deserve it, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They do not speak except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and he says what is right﴾. It is clear that intercession for the disbelievers is far from being right. Or: intercession does not benefit from the intercessors who are worthy of it in any state, except being for one to whom permission has been granted, that is, for his sake and concerning his affair, from among those deserving intercession. As for anyone other than them, who are not deserving of it, it benefits them not at all; even supposing its occurrence and its issuing from the intercessors, since they were not given permission to intercede for them, but only for others. Thus their deprivation of the intercession of these [intercessors] is established by the explicit wording of the text, and their deprivation of the intercession of the idols by its implication: since they are deprived of it from the side of those capable of interceding for some of those in need of it, then being deprived of it from the side of those incapable of it is all the more so. It has also been read: (uudhina lahu), in the passive voice.

﴿Until, when fear is removed from their hearts﴾. That is: the hearts of the intercessors and of those for whom intercession is made, from among the believers. As for the disbelievers, they are far from the station of seeking intercession, and far from having fear removed from their hearts by a thousand stations. "Tafzi'" means removing fear. Then he omitted mention of the fear and attributed the verb to the prepositional phrase. "Until" marks the endpoint of what the preceding clause indicates, namely the implication of permission being granted to those who are given it, for it is preceded by seeking permission, which calls for waiting and expectation of a reply, as if it were asked: "How are they given permission?" It was answered: they wait in the station of seeking permission and petitioning, and they stand still in dread and fear for a long time, until fear is removed from their hearts after much trepidation, and the first signs of the answer appear to them.

﴿They say﴾: that is, those for whom intercession is made, since they are the ones who need permission and are concerned with its matter: ﴿"What has your Lord said?"﴾ That is: concerning the matter of permission.

﴿They say﴾: that is, the intercessors, since they are the ones directly seeking permission, and the intermediaries between them and Him, mighty and majestic, through intercession.

﴿"The truth"﴾: that is, our Lord has said the true word, which is the permission to intercede for those deserving of it. It has also been read: (al-haqqu) in the nominative, meaning: what He said is the Truth.

﴿"And He is the Most High, the Most Great"﴾ is part of the speech of the intercessors, said in acknowledgment of the utmost greatness of the Presence of Might, mighty and majestic, and the inadequacy of the status of everyone other than Him. That is: He alone is singular in exaltedness and greatness; no one among the noblest of creatures may speak except by His permission. It has also been read: (fuzi'a), lightened, with the meaning of (fuzzi'a). It has been read: (fazi'a), with the verb in the active voice, its subject being God alone. It has been read: (furi'a), with the unpointed ra' and the pointed ghayn, meaning: the dread was removed from them; and "afna" from "faraghat al-zad" when nothing remains of it. This is a metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), since emptiness, which is "faragh," is the state of the container when it is exhausted, so it is attributed to it in reverse of the expression "jara al-nahr" (the river flowed). It is reported from al-Hasan that the ra' was lightened, and its original form is "faraga al-rajulu 'anha," meaning: he was free of it and it was exhausted; then the subject was deleted and the verb was attributed to the prepositional phrase, and by this the state of "tafrigh" is known. It has been read: (irtafa'a 'an qulubihim), with the meaning: it was uncovered from them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 24:

﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?"﴾ He (ﷺ) was commanded to rebuke the polytheists by bringing them to acknowledge that their deities do not possess an atom's weight in either of them, and that the Provider is God Most High, for they do not deny Him. This is what His saying, Most High, expresses: ﴿Say: "Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? Or who owns hearing and sight? And who brings the living out of the dead and brings the dead out of the living? And who directs the affair?" They will say, "God."﴾ Since they would sometimes hesitate in answering, fearing being forced into a corner, he (ﷺ) was told: ﴿Say: "God."﴾ For there is no other answer, equally so in their view.

﴿And indeed, we or you are surely upon guidance or in clear error.﴾ That is: one of the two parties, namely those who affirm the oneness of the One who alone provides, who possesses essential power, and who single Him out for worship, or those who associate with Him in worship inanimate matter situated at the lowest rank of possible existence, is surely upon one of the two states, guidance or clear error. This, following the eloquent demonstration that clearly specifies who is upon guidance and who is in error, is more forceful than explicit statement, since it proceeds according to the norms of fairness, which silence the most stubborn adversary. It has also been read: (وَإنّا أوْ إيّاكم إمّا عَلى هُدًى أوْ في ضَلالٍ مُبِينٍ) [wa-inna aw iyyakum la-'ala huda aw fi dalalin mubin]. The difference between the two prepositions (ʿalā and fī) serves to indicate that the one guided is like someone who has climbed a lighthouse and surveys things and looks out over them, while the one in error is as if immersed in darkness seeing nothing, or imprisoned in a pit unable to get out of it.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Say: You will not be asked about what we committed as sinners, and we will not be asked about what you do.﴾

This is more equitable and further from contention and unjust dispute, since here the criminality is attributed to the speaker (the believers) even though what is meant by it is a slip, while the more fitting attribution is left to themselves (the disbelievers), and mere "doing" is attributed to the addressees, even though their deeds are among the greatest of grave sins.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 26:

﴿Say: Our Lord will gather us together﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, at the time of the Gathering (hashr) and the Reckoning (hisab), ﴿then He will judge between us with truth﴾, i.e., He will decide between us and make a distinction after the true state of each of us and of you has become manifest, by admitting the people of truth (al-muhiqqun) to Paradise and the people of falsehood (al-mubtilun) to the Fire.

﴿And He is the Fattah﴾, the Judge (al-hakim) and the Decider (al-faysal) in matters that are closed off (al-qada'ya al-mun'aliqa), the All-Knowing (al-'alim) of what ought to be decided upon.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 27:

﴿Say: Show me those whom you have joined﴾ i.e., whom you have joined [to Him].

﴿with Him as partners﴾. The purpose of showing them, even though the idols are in plain view of him (ﷺ), is to make manifest the magnitude of their error and to make them aware of the falsehood of their opinion. That is, "Show them to me so that I may see by what attribute you have joined them with God, He to whom nothing is like, in deserving worship." This also contains further rebuke for them after the proof has been established against them. ﴿Nay﴾ is a rebuke to them against associating (partners), after the refutation of the comparison. ﴿Rather, He is God, the Mighty, the Wise﴾, i.e., the One described with overpowering dominance and dazzling wisdom. Where, then, are your partners, which are the basest and most abject of things, from this lofty rank? The pronoun [in "He"] is either referring to God, Exalted is He, or it is the pronoun of the matter (al-sha'n), as in: ﴿Say: He is God, One﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 28:

﴿And We have not sent you except comprehensively to mankind﴾. That is: except as a general mission to them. For when it encompasses them, it suffices them that none of them may escape it; or [it means]: except as one who gathers them together in the conveying [of the message]. Here it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the kāf (the pronoun "you" in "arsalnāka"), and the tā' is for emphasis (lil-mubālagha). There is no way to make it a circumstantial clause from "al-nās" (mankind), because it is impossible for a circumstantial clause to precede its referent when that referent is in the genitive (majrūr).

﴿as a bringer of good news and a warner, but most of mankind do not know﴾. That is: so their ignorance drives them to what they are upon of error and misguidance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 29:

﴿And they say﴾ out of the extreme of their ignorance and the utmost of their error: ﴿When is this promise﴾? By way of mockery, they mean by it the thing promised as good tidings and the thing warned of, or the promise made by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us in truth﴾.

﴿If you are truthful﴾, addressing the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers who follow him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 30:

﴿Say: For you is the appointment of a Day⦆ i.e., the promise of a day or a time. They (the grammarians) regarded the idafa (construct phrase) as explanatory (lil-tabyin). It is also read as (mi'adun yawmun), both nunated, in apposition (al-badal), and (yawman) with an implied verb, "a'nі" (I mean), for magnification (li-al-ta'zim).

﴿You will not be able to delay from it﴾ at the moment of its coming upon you, ﴿for an hour, nor will you be able to advance (it)﴾. The phrase is a description of "mi'ad" (appointment). In this reply there is an exaggeration in the threat that is not hidden, since it made delaying (istí'khar) as impossible as advancing (istiqdam), which is rationally impossible; and its explanation has passed several times. It is also permissible that the negation of delaying and advancing is not restricted to the moment of its sudden arrival, so the description of the appointment with this is for confirming it (tahqiqihi) and establishing it (taqririhi). (p-134)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 31:

﴿And those who disbelieve say: "We will never believe in this Qur'an, nor in that which is before it."﴾ That is: of the earlier scriptures that point to the Resurrection (al-ba'th). It has also been said: the disbelievers of Makkah asked the People of the Book about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they informed them that they found his description in their books. So they became angry and said that. It has also been said: "that which is before it" refers to the Final Hour (al-qiyamah).

﴿And if only you could see when the wrongdoers﴾ — those who deny the Resurrection — ﴿are made to stand before their Lord﴾. That is: at the station of reckoning (al-muhasabah).

﴿They exchange words among themselves﴾. That is: they argue with one another and send back words to each other (yataraja'una al-qawl).

﴿Those who were deemed weak will say﴾ — this is a substitute (badal) for "yarji'u" ... etc. That is: the followers will say,

﴿to those who were arrogant﴾ in the world, and who led them into error and misguidance: ﴿"Had it not been for you"﴾. That is: had it not been for your misleading us and your turning us away from faith, ﴿"we would have been believers"﴾ by following the Messenger (ﷺ).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 32:

﴿Those who were arrogant said to those who were oppressed﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) built upon a question, as if it were said: "What did those who were arrogant say in reply?" So it is said: they said: ﴿Did we turn you away from the guidance after it had come to you? Rather, you were criminals﴾, denying that they were the ones who barred them from faith, and affirming that they themselves were the ones who barred themselves, because they were firmly rooted in criminality.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 33:

﴿And those who were oppressed will say to those who were arrogant﴾ (this is) a turning away from their (the arrogant's) turning away (idrab) and a nullification of it (ibtal): ﴿Nay, it was the scheming of the night and the day﴾. That is: nay, your scheming against us by night and by day diverted us. The genitive complement (al-mudaf ilayhi) has been omitted, and the adverbial noun (al-zarf) has been put in its place by extension (ittisa'). Or, their night and their day are made the schemers by way of metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi). It is also read: ﴿Nay, scheming of the night and the day﴾ with tanwin and with the two adverbs in the accusative (bal makrun al-layla wa-l-nahara), meaning: nay, your scheming diverted us in the night and the day, on the basis that the tanwin is a substitute (iwad) for the omitted genitive complement; or (it means) a great scheming, on the basis that it is for magnification (li-l-tafkhim). It is also read: ﴿Nay, scheming of the night and the day﴾ (bal makru al-layli wa-l-nahara) with the nominative and the accusative, meaning: you pursue seduction with a constant scheming from which you never cease. The nominative is in the agentive function (al-fa'iliyya), meaning: nay, your scheming, the seduction in the night and the day, diverted us, according to what preceded regarding the extension in the adverb by placing it in the position of the genitive complement. The accusative is in the verbal-noun function (al-masdariyya), meaning: nay, you pursue seduction with the scheming of the night and the day, that is, a constant scheming. And His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when you were commanding us﴾ (idh ta'murunana) is an adverbial clause (zarf) modifying the scheming, meaning: nay, your constant scheming at the time of your commanding us.

﴿to disbelieve in God and set up rivals to Him﴾ (an nakfura billahi wa-naj'ala lahu andadan). On the basis that their scheming refers either to the very act of their commanding with what is mentioned, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O my people, remember the favour of God upon you when He appointed prophets among you and made you kings﴾, for the two appointments mentioned are a favour from God, exalted is He, and what a favour! Or (it refers to) other matters accompanying their command that call to compliance with it, such as encouragement and intimidation and other things. (p-135)

﴿And they concealed their regret when they saw the punishment﴾ (wa-asarru al-nadamata lamma ra'aw al-'adhab). That is: both groups harboured regret over what they had done of misguidance and misleading, and each of them concealed it from the other out of fear of reproach. Or they displayed it, since (the verb asarra) is among the words with contrary meanings (al-adhdad), and this is the one that fits their state.

﴿And We put shackles on the necks of those who disbelieved﴾ (wa-ja'alna al-aghlala fi a'naqi alladhina kafaru). That is: on their necks. The explicit noun (al-idhar) is used in place of the pronoun (al-idmar) to draw attention to their blame and to point out the cause of their shackles.

﴿Are they being recompensed except for what they used to do?﴾ (hal yujzawna illa ma kanu ya'malun). That is: they are not recompensed except with a recompense for what they used to do; or, except by what they used to do, with the preposition elided (ala naz' al-jarr).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 34:

﴿Never did We send a warner to a town﴾ from among the towns.

﴿but its affluent ones said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾ This is a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he suffered from his people of denial and disbelief in what he brought, and of rivalry through the abundance of wealth and children, and of boasting through the portions and adornments of this world, and of arrogance over the believers on account of that, and of belittling them for his sake. And their saying: ﴿Which of the two groups is better in station and finer in assembly?﴾ [Q. 19:73] — that no warner was ever sent to the people of any town but "its affluent ones said," just as the affluent ones of the people of Makkah said concerning him (ﷺ), and they plotted against him in the same way they plotted against him (ﷺ), and they measured the matters of the Hereafter, which were imagined and presumed by them, by the matters of this world, and they claimed that if they were not honored by Allah Most High, He would not have given them the good things of this world, and that were it not that the believers were despised by Him, Most High, they would not have been deprived of them. And upon that feeble opinion they built their rulings.

And they say, "We have more wealth and children, and we will not be punished." This is either on the basis of the outright denial of the punishment of the Hereafter, or on the belief that God, exalted is He, has honored them in this world, so He will not humiliate them in the Hereafter, assuming it occurs.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (*Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim*) on surah 34, verse 36:

﴿Say﴾, as a rebuttal to them, a cutting off of the root of their vain greed, and a confirmation of the truth upon which the affair of creation (*al-takwin*) turns.

﴿Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whom He wills﴾ to extend it for him, ﴿and restricts it﴾ for whom He wills to restrict it, without there being any reason for either of the two groups to be the cause of what is done to them of extension or restriction. Thus He may expand provision for the disobedient and restrict it for the obedient, He may reverse the matter, He may expand it for both of them together, He may restrict it for both of them, and He may expand it for one person at one time and restrict it for him at another. He does each of these according to what His will requires, a will grounded in far-reaching wisdoms. Therefore, the matter of reward and punishment, whose basis is obedience and its absence, is not to be measured by this. It was also recited as (*wa-yuqaddiru*), with the doubled letter (*bi-l-tashdid*), i.e. with the intensive form of the verb.

﴿But most people do not know﴾ this, so they suppose that the basis of extension is nobility and honour, and the basis of restriction is humiliation. They do not realise that the former is often by way of *istidraj* (gradual lead-on, a respite that leads to ruin), and the latter by way of *ibtila'* (trial) and the raising of ranks.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 37:

﴿And it is not your wealth nor your children that will bring you near to Us in nearness.﴾ (p-136) This is a resumed statement from Him, exalted and majestic be He, addressed to the people by way of variation (talwin) and shifting of address (iltifat), for the sake of emphasizing the truth and affirming what preceded. That is: the group of your wealth and the group of your children are not the group that will bring you near to Us in nearness. For the broken plural (jam' mukassar), its rational and non-rational referents are equal in the rule of feminine gender, or [it means]: not by the quality that brings you near. It has also been read as (بِالَّذِي), that is, "by the thing which" (بِالشَّيْءِ الَّذِي).

﴿Except for those who believe and do righteous deeds.﴾ This is an exception from the object of tuqarribukum (bring you near), that is: wealth and children bring no one near except the righteous believer who spent his wealth in the way of Allah, taught his children goodness, raised them upon righteousness, and prepared them for obedience. It has also been said: "from your wealth and your children" with the elision of a modifier (mudaf), that is: except the wealth of one who... etc.

﴿Those﴾ is a reference to "man" (من), and the plural is in consideration of its meaning, just as the singular in the two verbs is in consideration of its wording. The sense of distance together with the nearness of the time of the one referred to is for signifying the loftiness of their rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence, that is: those described with faith and righteous deeds.

﴿For them is the recompense of the multiplied (ad-dij'f)﴾ meaning: it is established for them. That is, the prepositional phrase is a predicate of what follows it, and the clause is a predicate of "those", and in it is emphasis through the repetition of the predication. Or: it establishes that for them, with the prepositional phrase as predicate of "those", and what follows it being raised as the subject. The annexation of "recompense" to "the multiplied" is an annexation of the verbal noun to its object; its original form was: "they shall be recompensed the multiple," then "the recompense of the multiple," then "the recompense of the multiple." Its meaning is that their single good deed is multiplied for them tenfold and more. It has been read as jaza'an (recompense, accusative) with ad-dij'f as the subject, on the reading (فَأُولَئِكَ لَهُمُ الضِّعْفُ جَزاءً), and (جَزاءً الضِّعْفُ) on the sense that they are recompensed the multiple, and (جَزاءُ الضِّعْفِ) with nominative, on the basis that ad-dij'f is an apposition (badal) of jaza'.

﴿For what they did﴾ of righteous deeds, ﴿and they will be in the chambers﴾ that is, the chambers of Paradise.

﴿Secure﴾ from all hardships. It has been read with a fatha and with a sukun on the ra', and it has been read (فِي الغُرْفَةِ) in the sense of the genus.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 38:

﴿And those who strive against Our signs﴾ by rejecting and disparaging them, ﴿seeking to frustrate [Us]﴾, outstripping Our messengers, or supposing that they can escape Us.

﴿Those shall be brought forth to the punishment﴾, and what they relied upon will avail them nothing.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 39:

﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord extends provision to whomever He wills of His servants﴾ That is: He expands it for him at times.

﴿and restricts it for him﴾ That is: He constricts it for him at other times. So do not fear poverty, spend in the way of Allah, and expose yourselves to His gifts (nafahat), exalted is He.

﴿And whatever you spend of anything, He will replace it﴾ with a substitute, either in this world quickly or in the next world later.

﴿And He is the best of providers﴾ For others are only intermediaries in conveying His provision; there is no true reality to their being providers.

﴿And on the Day He gathers them all together﴾, i.e., the arrogant and the weak. "And what they used to worship besides Allah." "Yawm" (the Day) is an adverb of time (ẓarf) governing an implied verb that comes later, whose estimate will be stated, or it is the object of an implied verb placed earlier, such as "udhkur" (remember).

﴿Then He will say to the angels: "Are these the ones who used to worship you?"﴾ This is a rebuke to the polytheists and a silencing of them, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Did you say to the people, "Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah"?﴾ ... and so on. It is also a dashing of their hopes, which they had vainly pinned on their intercession. The angels are singled out because they are the most noble of their associates and the ones fit to be addressed among them, and because their worship is the origin of polytheism.
