Thus, by showing the angels' inadequacy to the rank of being worshipped, and their disassociation from being worshipped, the condition of all their other associates is made evident by way of greater priority. Both verbs were also read with the nūn (the first person plural, "We").

"They say," is a resumption answering an implied question arising from the narration of the angels' question. It is as if it were said: "What will the angels say then?" So it is said: "They say, exalting Him above that: ﴿Glory be to You; You are our Walī (Protector) apart from them﴾." The shift to the past form (ṣīghat al-māḍī) indicates certainty; that is, "You are the One whom we take as our ally apart from them, with no alliance between us and them." It is as if by this they declared their disavowal of approving of their worship. Then they turned away from that and denied that they had truly worshipped them, by saying: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, i.e., the devils, inasmuch as they obeyed them in worshipping other than Allah, glorified and exalted is He. It is also said: they used to appear to them in forms and imagine to them that they were the angels, so they worshipped them; and it is also said: they would enter the bellies of the idols when they were worshipped, and so they would be worshipped through their worship.

﴿Most of them believed in them﴾: The first pronoun refers to mankind or to the polytheists, and "most" (al-akthar) means "all"; the second pronoun refers to the jinn.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 42:

﴿So on that Day none of you will have power to benefit or harm one another﴾ is part of what is said to the angels when they respond by declaring their transcendence and disavowal of what the disbelievers attributed to them. They are addressed with this before the assembled witnesses (ru'us al-ashhad), to manifest their impotence and inadequacy in the eyes of their worshippers, and to state explicitly what entails the complete disappointment of their hopes. The "fa'" (fa, "so") is not for ordering what follows from the judgment concerning the angels' response, since it is established whether or not they answered with that. Rather, it is for ordering the report of it upon that (the response). The attribution of the absence of benefit and harm to an indefinite "some" (al-ba'd al-mubham) serves to intensify what is intended, which is the explanation of the angels' lack of benefit to the worshippers, by placing it in the same line as the worshippers' lack of benefit to them, as if the angels' benefit to their worshippers is as impossible and non-existent as the worshippers' benefit to them. The mention of the absence of harm, although there is no inquiry into it at all, is either to generalize the impotence, or to read the absence of benefit as referring to the case of worship and the absence of harm as referring to the case of abandoning it, or because what is meant is the repelling of harm, with an elided genitive (hadhf al-mudaf). The restriction of this ruling to that Day, although it holds absolutely, is because their hope was founded on the realization of benefit on that day.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And We will say to those who did wrong﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon "We will say to the angels," not upon "none will have power," as has been said. For it is among what is said on the Day of Resurrection, addressed to the angels, following upon their reported response. This is a narration by the Messenger (ﷺ) of what will be said to the worshippers on that day, following the narration of what will be said to the angels; that is: on the day We gather them all, then We will say to the angels such and such, and they will say: such and such, and We will say to the polytheists: ﴿Taste the punishment of the Fire which you used to deny﴾. There will be, of the terrors and conditions, what the scope of speech cannot encompass. And His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 43:

﴿And when Our clear signs are recited to them﴾ (p-138) is an explanation of some other part of their disbelief; that is, when Our signs that declare the truth of monotheism (tawhid) and the falsehood of association (shirk) are recited to them by the tongue of the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿They say: "This is not"﴾ meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿"but a man who wants to turn you away from what your fathers used to worship"﴾ so that he may gather you to what he calls to, without there being any divine religion behind it. The attribution of the fathers to the addressees, rather than to themselves, is to stir up the vein of tribal zeal in them; it is an exaggeration in confirming them upon polytheism and in repelling them from monotheism.

﴿And they say: "This is not"﴾ meaning the noble Qur'an.

﴿"but a fabrication"﴾ that is, speech turned away from its proper course, having no correspondence to reality,

﴿"invented"﴾ by attributing it to Allah, the Exalted. ﴿And those who disbelieved say of the truth﴾ that is, of the matter of prophethood, or of Islam, or of the Qur'an. The conjunction here is due to a difference in designation, such that the first refers to its meaning and the second to its inimitable composition.

﴿When it has come to them﴾ without any reflection or contemplation upon it.

﴿"This is nothing but clear magic"﴾ its being magic is evident. The repetition of the verb, the explicit mention of the disbelievers, the indication in the two lams to the speakers and the one spoken of, and the haste in "lamma" to pronounce this false saying definitively, all constitute a great denial of it and an eloquent expression of astonishment at it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 44:

﴿And We did not give them any books which they study﴾. In this there is evidence for the falsity of associationism (shirk), as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority, so that it speaks of what they used to associate with Him?﴾, and His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they hold fast to it?﴾ It is also read: (yadrusunaha) and (yaddarisunaha) with the letter dal doubled, of the form yafta'iluna, from al-dars (study).

﴿And We did not send to them before you any warner﴾ calling them to it, and warning them of punishment if they do not associate partners with Him. It has already become clear before this that there is no justification for it in any way whatsoever, so from where did they derive this deviant course? This is the utmost ignorance attributed to them and a demonstration of the foolishness of their opinion. Then He threatened them with His saying, Exalted is He:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 45:**

﴿And those before them denied,﴾ among the earlier nations and the bygone generations. ﴿As they denied, and they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them,﴾ meaning: these people did not reach a tenth of the strength, long life and abundance of wealth that We gave those (earlier ones); or, those (earlier ones) did not reach a tenth of what We gave these (later ones) of clear proofs and guidance.

﴿So they denied My messengers﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "those who denied"... and so on, by way of detail and explanation, like His exalted words: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, so they denied Our servant﴾... and so on.

﴿So how was My rejection?﴾ That is: My rejecting them by destruction. So let these people beware of the like of that.

﴿Say: I only admonish you with one thing﴾. That is: I only guide you and counsel you with one matter, which is what His words indicate: ﴿that you stand up for God﴾. This phrase may be a *badal* (substitution, in grammar: an apposition replacing the preceding word) of "one thing," or a *bayan* (explanatory apposition) of it, or the *khabar* (predicate) of an omitted *mubtada'* (subject), meaning: it is that you stand up [to leave] the assembly of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or that you stand up for the matter sincerely for the sake of God, Exalted, turning away from *mira'* (disputation) and *taqlid* (blind imitation).

﴿Two by two and singly﴾. That is: scattered, two by two and one by one. Crowding confuses understanding and mixes thoughts with delusions. Placing *mathna* (two by two) first indicates that it is more reliable and closer to tranquility.

﴿Then you reflect﴾ on his matter (ﷺ) and what he has brought, so that you may know its reality and its truth. His words, Exalted is He, ﴿There is no madness in your companion﴾, are a *isti'naf* (resumptive new clause) directed from Him, Exalted, to alert to the method of observation and contemplation: that such a great matter, under which lies the sovereignty of this world and the Hereafter, is not claimed except by a madman, who does not care about being exposed when challenged for proof and his incapacity becomes apparent; or by one supported by God, qualified for prophethood, confident in his argument and proof. Since you know that he (ﷺ) is the most intelligent of all people in reason, the most truthful in speech, the purest in soul, the most excellent in knowledge, the best in deed, and the most comprehensive of human perfections, it is necessary that you believe him in his claim. How much more so, since miracles that would make the solid mountains tremble have been added to that?

It is also permissible that it be linked to what precedes it, meaning: "Then you reflect, so that you know that there is no madness in your companion." It has also been allowed that *ma* be interrogative, meaning: "Then you reflect: what sign of madness is in him?"

﴿He is only a warner to you before a severe punishment﴾. This is the punishment of the Hereafter, for he (ﷺ) is sent at the very approach of the Hour.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 47:

﴿Say: "Whatever reward I have asked of you⁠—﴾ that is: whatever reward I have asked of you for the message.

﴿then it is for yourselves.﴾ The intended meaning is the outright negation of asking. It is like the saying of one who says to someone he has not given anything: "If I have given you anything, then take it." It was also said: "ma" (whatever) is a relative pronoun, meaning what he asked them, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I do not ask of you any reward for it, except that whoever wills may take a path to his Lord﴾, and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I do not ask of you any reward for it, except love for kinship﴾. Taking a path to Him, exalted is He, is their greatest benefit, and his kinship (ﷺ) is their kinship.

﴿My reward is only from Allah, and He is over all things Witness.﴾ He is Observer, who knows my truthfulness and the sincerity of my intention. It was also read: (inni ajri) with the ya' (of "ajri") silent.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 48:

﴿Say: Indeed, my Lord hurls the truth﴾, i.e., He casts it down and sends it upon whomever He chooses from among His servants. Or it means: He hurls the truth at falsehood, so it crushes it (yadmaghuhu). Or it means: He hurls it into the far corners of the horizons, so that it becomes a promise of the manifestation of Islam and the elevation of the word of truth.

﴿Knower of the unseen﴾: this is an attribute carried over to the place of "inna" and its noun (i.e., it is in the grammatical position of the noun of inna), or it is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun hidden in "yaqdhifu", or it is a second predicate (khabar thani) of "inna", or it is the predicate of an omitted subject (mubtada' mahdhuf). It has also been read in the accusative (naṣb) as an attribute of "rabbi", or as an implied "a'ni" (I mean). It has also been read with the ghayn kasra (ʿallāmi l-ghuyūbi, "ghuyūb" with kasra in the form), and with fatha as "ṣabūr" in the form of an intensive (mubalagha) of the absent (ghā'ib), with the same meaning.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 49:

﴿Say: The truth has come﴾, i.e., Islam and Tawhid (divine oneness). ﴿And falsehood neither originates nor restores﴾, i.e., shirk (association of partners with God) has vanished such that no trace of it remains at all. It is derived from the destruction of a living being, for when it perishes, it no longer has any origination (ibda') or restoration (i'adah). Thus it is used as an example of complete annihilation. From this is the verse of ʿUbayd:

؎ Ughayyid has been emptied of its people, so it neither originates nor restores

It was also said: the falsehood is Iblis or the idol, and the meaning is that it does not create any creation, nor does it restore; or it does not originate any good for its people, nor does it restore. It was also said: "ma" is interrogative, in the accusative case, governed by the verb after it.

Say: "If I go astray, I only go astray to my own detriment. So the burden of my straying falls upon myself, because it is due to it (the self), for it is the one that is ignorant of its essence and the one that commands to evil. And in accordance with this consideration, the conditional clause is paired with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if I am guided, it is because of what my Lord reveals to me﴾, because being guided is by His guidance and His enabling success. It has also been read as (rabbiya) with a fatha on the ya'. ﴿Indeed He is Hearing, Near﴾ (p-140), who knows the speech and the action of each of the one who is guided and the one who is astray, even if they conceal them."

"And if you could see when they are terrified" at the time of death, or at the Resurrection, or on the day of Badr.

It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that eighty thousand men will raid the Ka'bah to destroy it; when they enter al-Bayda', they will be swallowed up by the earth. The answer to "law" (if) is omitted, meaning: you would see a terrifying matter.

﴿So there will be no escape﴾: they will not escape Allah, Mighty and Majestic, by flight or by taking refuge.

﴿And they will be seized from a near place﴾: from the surface of the earth, or from the place of standing (on the Day of Resurrection) to the Fire, or from the plain of Badr to its well, or from beneath their feet when they are swallowed up. The clause is conjoined to "they were terrified." It has also been said that it is conjoined to "no escape," meaning: when they were terrified, they did not escape, and they were seized. This is supported by the reading (wa-akhdhun, "and a seizing"), in conjunction with its place (grammatical position), meaning: there is no escape here or there, and there is a seizing.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 34, verse 52:**

﴿And they say, "We believe in him."﴾ That is, in Muhammad (ﷺ), whose mention has passed in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your companion is not mad﴾.

﴿And how can they reach [it] from a distant place?﴾ *Al-tanawush* (التَّناوُشُ) is the easy taking hold of something, meaning: and from where for them [is there] the taking hold of faith in an easy manner? ﴿From a distant place﴾, for it lies within the realm of obligation (taklif), and they are at a far remove from it. This is a parable of their state in seeking to obtain faith after it has escaped them, and it is likened to the state of one who wishes to take hold of a thing from a distance beyond the range of a reach of a cubit, which is impossible.

It has also been read with a hamza (*al-tanaush*, التَّناؤُشُ), by way of changing the waw into a hamza because of its damma. It derives from *na'ashtu al-shay'* (نَأشْتُ الشَّيْءَ), when you seek it. And it is related from Abu 'Amr that *al-tana'ush* (التَّناؤُشُ) with a hamza means taking hold from a distance, from their saying: *na'ashtu* (نَأشْتُ), when I delayed and was late. From this is the saying of one who said:

؎ He wished, too late, that he had obeyed me, and [yet] after affairs have come to pass, things have happened.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 53:

﴿And they had already disbelieved in it﴾, i.e., in Muhammad (ﷺ), or in the severe punishment with which he warned them.

﴿Before﴾, i.e., before that, in the time of accountability (al-taklif, the period of being charged with religious obligations).

﴿And they hurl [accusations] at the unseen﴾: they pelt with conjecture and speak about the Messenger (ﷺ) with slanders that had not become apparent to them, or about the punishment mentioned, pronouncing definitively that it does not exist.

﴿From a far-off place﴾: from a remote position regarding his (ﷺ) state, since they attribute to him (ﷺ) poetry, magic and lying. Indeed, the thing furthest from what he brought is poetry and magic, and the thing furthest from his well-known habit, in the eyes of near and far alike, is lying. Perhaps this is an illustration of their situation in this matter by the situation of one who throws at something he does not see from a far-off place, where there is no room for the illusion that it reaches it. It has also been read (qira'a, a recognized variant reading): ﴿and they hurl [accusations]﴾, on the basis that Satan casts [these things] to them and instructs them in that. This is coordinated with ﴿they had already disbelieved in it﴾, as a narration of a past state, or with ﴿they say﴾, so that it becomes an illustration of their situation by the situation of one who hurls, in attaining what they had squandered of faith in the world.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 34, verse 54:**

﴿And they will be prevented from what they desire﴾, namely the benefit of faith and deliverance from the Fire. It is also read with *ishmam* (a partial rounding of the lips, signalling the *damma* without fully pronouncing it) on the *ḥā'* (الحاء).

﴿As was done with their counterparts before﴾, that is, with their likes among the disbelieving nations of the bygone.

﴿Indeed, they were in disquieting doubt﴾, that is, causing suspicion (مُوقِعٍ في الرِّيبَةِ), or possessing suspicion (ذِي رِيبَةٍ). The first reading is transferred from what can truly be described as disquieting (مُرِيبًا) among concrete things to the meaning, and the second is from the one who has doubt to the doubt itself, as in the saying "poetry of a poet" (شِعْرُ شاعِرٍ). And God knows best.

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah Saba', there will not remain any messenger or prophet except that he will be a companion and one who shakes hands with him on the Day of Resurrection."
